 WATCH: Zelenskyy confirms Ukraine hacked back after Russia's cyberattack of its emergency alert system
 World 
 Updated on Nov 2, 2026 4:47 PM EST — Published on
 Nov 2, 2026 1:06 PM EST
 Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed that his country retaliated against Russia by hacking its emergency alert system.
 "We only respond on their attacks," Zelenskyy said in an interview with PBS News' Amna Nawaz.
 The cyberattack, the Ukrainian leader said, was a response to Russia seemingly hacking Ukraine's emergency alert system, which notifies residents of imminent threats.
 "They attacked our system," he said. "It was a cyberattack."
 READ MORE: Ukraine and Russia both report fake emergency alerts after cyberattacks target apps as limited ceasefire ends 
 Ukrainian authorities said on Sunday that users received false warnings of an imminent nuclear threat on their emergency alert mobile app. The alert system was suspended but is now back up and running.
 SUPPORT PBS NEWS: Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass 
 "When it was very clear … that it's their personal attack against our people, civilians," Zelenskyy said. "Of course, we responded."
 Russian authorities on Monday said hackers gained access to their emergency mobile app and sent fake emergency alerts.
 Here are other key takeaways from his interview with PBS News.
 Zelenskyy describes his relationship with Trump as 'emotional'
 When Nawaz asked Zelenskyy to describe his relationship with President Donald Trump in one word, Zelenskyy paused.
 "Emotional," he said.
 Trump has previously described Zelenskyy as "not a good guy," and has said he shouldn't be the Ukrainian president and doesn't want an end to the war.
 WATCH: Ukraine less reliant on U.S. as Trump-Zelenskyy rift deepens, former ambassador says 
 Following the release of an American imprisoned in Russia, U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff described Putin as a "humanitarian." Putin has been indicted for war crimes by the International Criminal Court.
 WATCH: American imprisoned by Russia released as Witkoff meets and praises Putin 
 "Sometimes we need to be pragmatic in this war," Zelenskyy said. "Who is an enemy? Who began this war? Putin. Don't find good words to describe him. I'm not sure that it will be helpful."
 Zelenskyy also criticized Trump's deal with Russia to import tons of Russian diesel to the U.S.
 "If you are really about money, business and pragmatism, so don't speak that it will have influence on the price in the United States," Zelenskyy said. "No, it's not true, it doesn't work."
 WATCH: Ukraine disputes Trump's claim of energy ceasefire as Russian diesel deal draws fire 
 Experts say it's unlikely the deal will reduce global diesel prices in the near future.
 The Ukrainian president told Nawaz the pragmatic thing to do is to support Ukraine.
 "We have to support Ukraine," he said. "Because it has to be strong, because otherwise Putin will go further to Europe and to the different parts of NATO countries."
 Zelenskyy has asked Trump to reduce limits to Ukraine's use of Starshield
 Zelenskyy said he has asked Trump several times to reduce limits to Ukraine's use of Starshield, a military-grade version of Starlink satellite internet service. The system is funded by the Pentagon and operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX.
 Starshield, which is a key component of Ukraine's military communications network, has geographic restrictions. It can't be used to carry out attacks inside Russia. It can act defensively and in the Russian occupied territories of Ukraine.
 Zelenskyy said if given the opportunity, Ukraine would use the system to identify and attack missile launch sites inside Russia. He said Ukraine would not use Starshield to carry out massive attacks on Russia or energy sites due to the likelihood of civilian casualties.
 Lifting Starshield limits would mean Russia wouldn't "have opportunity to use each day ballistic missiles against us," Zelenskyy said. "Because we will block their launches."
 The Ukrainian president said Trump seemed open to the reduction of limits.
 "He said that he will try. It doesn't depend on him," Zelenskyy said. "He said that it depends mostly on SpaceX. He said that he's supportive, and I was very thankful."
 In mid-October, Starshield was partially disabled. The details of what happened are unclear .
 WATCH: How Starlink disruptions affected Ukraine's battlefield operations 
 Musk said limits to Starshield's speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and Trump. Trump has said he didn't order the restrictions and doubted that Musk was to blame for the disruption.
 Asked who he thought was to blame for the disruption, Zelenskyy said he's unsure whether Musk can act alone.
 "I'm not sure that he can do it with Starshield because it's military. It's government version," Zelenskyy said. "I'm not sure that he could do it personally alone without any representatives from American government."
 Asked whether he believes Musk supports Ukraine and wants it to win the war, Zelenskyy said "I don't know."
 He said he wanted to speak with Musk following the Starshield disruptions but "they didn't connect with us."
 See more of our interview with Zelenskyy on Monday's PBS News Hour.
